rewrites.summary:
In 2024 a trans woman was the victim of an attempted femicide (femicidio frustrado) in Punta Arenas, the regional capital: the tribunal imposed four years against the five years the prosecution had requested, an under-sentence for gender-motivated violence against a trans woman that is a concrete severity finding for a visitor assessing protection in this region. In April 2026 the regional director of SernamEG, the national women and gender-equality service, publicly criticised the sentence as not reflecting the gravity of the attack and announced an appeal — a named institutional pushback that partially offsets the judicial under-penalisation.

For a visitor, the practical exposure here is low absolute case volume, but the judicial precedent of reduced sentences for attacks on trans women is a severity signal that keeps the risk assessment below the national baseline.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The national comparison frames the finding: at −0.06 against the national 0.72, the deviation is small, and the appeal is the counter-signal that prevents a deeper deduction. Compared with its neighbour Tarapacá (0.64), this region is 0.02 higher: Tarapacá's court annulment voids the femicide protection entirely for trans women in that jurisdiction, whereas this region applied the femicide framework but under-sentenced, and the national service is actively appealing to correct the record.
rewrites.localsOnly: The case itself is resident-facing: the victim, Kenia Chacón, is a trans woman attacked in Punta Arenas in 2024, and her mother publicly denounced the devaluation of the attack on the basis of her daughter's gender identity. On the dataset, Magallanes appeared among the regions with the largest percentage increases in 2024 and holds 0.96 % of the national case total.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The April 2026 appeal is an announced step rather than a decided outcome; its result is not documented in this record. The dataset rise figures are as reported by the annual report and not independently verified here. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

rewrites.summary: The Court of Appeals of Iquique annulled the entire trial over the killing of a transgender woman, holding that the femicide (femicidio) offence — the strongest gendered-violence protection in Chile's penal code — covers only "a person biologically female" and therefore the conviction could not stand as framed. The annulment was delivered in this region, where the Iquique court exercises jurisdiction, and it is a named judicial finding that in Tarapacá the most severe legal protection for gender-motivated violence does not extend to trans women. For a trans person assaulted in Tarapacá, the operative judicial reading leaves a concrete protection gap: the strongest enforcement tool for gendered violence is unavailable on that reading even though the legal framework remains on the books nationally.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.08 deviation in the scored set — a small-share region at 1.56 % of the national anti-LGBTI case total in 2024, in which a single structural finding dominates the per-capita signal. Compared with its neighbour La Araucanía (0.65), Tarapacá is 0.01 lower: Araucanía's −0.07 is trend-based (+150 % rise, low visibility), whereas Tarapacá carries a specific court ruling that names trans women as outside the femicide definition. Compared with a further neighbour, Arica y Parinacota (0.69), Tarapacá is 0.05 lower because the Iquique annulment is a documented finding within Tarapacá's own judicial district, whereas Arica's deviation rests on the shared northern-court context with no trans-specific incident of its own.
rewrites.localsOnly: Case details are resident-facing: the victim was Yuri Pizarro, a 55-year-old trans woman whose body was found on the coast of the provincial capital in June 2022; her killer, Jhonatan Cañon, was convicted at first instance to presidio perpetuo (a lifetime sentence), and on the defence's nullity motion the Iquique court declared the sentence void in early October 2023. Tarapacá accounted for 1.56 % of the national anti-LGBTI case total in 2024, a small-share region whose resident case count a single structural finding dominates.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The annulment records one appellate court's reading; whether it marks a settled interpretation across the region's judiciary is not established in this record, and no follow-up ruling is documented. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

rewrites.summary:
Cyprus is a country workable for trans visitors. The legal framework is mid-transition: public incitement to hatred based on gender identity is a criminal offence (2015), and gender identity is an aggravating factor in hate crime (2017). A legal gender recognition bill (self-determination basis) was approved by the Council of Ministers in September 2022 and is pending in parliament; until it passes, legal gender recognition requires surgery under the 2002 Civil Registry Law — a resident-facing arrangement.

No traveler-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues for an EU member, and tourist infrastructure is Western-standard and accustomed to diverse visitors. Gender identity is not yet an explicit ground in the non-discrimination framework. The divided country matters: the northern part operates under a de facto Turkish-controlled administration with a weaker protection regime and less documentation, and travelers should treat the north as closer to a riskier profile than the south, where these protections apply.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Reform promise and legislative layers colour the framework: the September 2022 legal recognition bill (self-determination basis, first parliamentary reading in November 2022) is the outstanding implementation step after its 2019 UPR — the country accepted all eight SOGIESC recommendations and promised correction of registered sex based on a registrar's decision, without prior medical intervention. The protections arrived in layers: criminalisation of incitement in 2013, extension of the offence in 2015, a 2017 aggravating-factor law, and a 2023 conversion-practices ban. Gender identity is not yet an explicit ground in the non-discrimination framework; the country joined a rights coalition in August 2018, and a European human-rights body has urged a gender-identity ground.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The pending self-determination LGR bill and the current surgery requirement under the 2002 Civil Registry Law are resident-facing.

The northern part of the country runs its own recognition process requiring surgical proof, and gender identity is not yet an explicit ground in the non-discrimination framework — both resident-facing features.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The north/south division of the country into two parts and the pending LGR bill are noted; LGR requirements are resident-facing. The bill's final status is pending as of the reporting dates; the training and the conversion-practices ban are noted from their reporting sources. Traveller-facing conclusions here describe the southern part where these protections apply; conditions in the northern part are less documented. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

A national network country report on gender equality (2024) records how the national equal-treatment rules are transposed into this country's law, including identity-related aspects of the framework.

A civil-society booklet documents gender-recognition practice on the divided country: recognition runs on self-determination without psychiatric or surgical gatekeeping, one part runs its own recognition process, and a confidential support line operates daily covering identity, work, family, shelter, health and military-service issues.

A report on a review session (January 2019) records that the country received eight identity-related recommendations and accepted all of them; its national report promised new legislation for correcting registered sex requiring only a registrar's decision, with no prior medical intervention; a human-rights body had urged identity as a prohibited discrimination ground; and the country joined a rights coalition in August 2018.
A legal experts' country report on non-discrimination (2020) records the transposition of the national equal-treatment rules, including identity grounds in this country's law.

A news report (October 2013) records that the penal code was amended to criminalise incitement to violence or hatred based on identity, punishable by up to three years' imprisonment and/or a fine, with workplace identity protections added earlier.

rewrites.summary:
Ecuador is a country that demands real caution from trans visitors. Legal gender recognition has existed since 2016, and the legal framework is now among the region's strongest. The 2024 reform lets adults change name and sex/gender on the identity document directly through the civil registry (one time, no surgery), and in 2024-25 court rulings extended document changes to trans adolescents and reprimanded the legislature for stalling trans-rights implementation.

The violence side is severe: a monitoring group documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023 with inadequate state response, and the "internal armed conflict" against gangs has intensified general violence since January 2024, with two more LGBTQ people killed in its first weeks; Quito and Guayaquil, the two main cities, carry real street risk, and police capacity is consumed by the security crisis.

For a visitor: documents and expression are legally protected, but the probability of encountering violence if outed in public is among the highest in the region right now.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The framework's bedrock is the adjacent layer: the 2008 constitution's non-discrimination foundation (including sexual orientation and identity), the 2019 marriage-equality ruling, and a 2018 court order requiring the civil registry to register the child of a same-sex couple. Dated official context: a 2011 human-rights report documented discrimination based on sexual orientation among broader societal problems, and the platform notes that same-sex couples remain barred from adoption by a constitutional ban.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The 2024 Civil Registry reform and the adolescent document-change rulings are resident-facing; the 27-murder toll and its inadequate state response fall on residents.

The adolescent rulings arose from a specific teenager's case that opened the path for other adolescents seeking legal recognition, and the 2024 reform's operative procedure came via the 2024 regulation of the identity law.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The general security emergency affects all travelers; the score reflects the trans-specific legal/violence balance. The murder toll is a single organisation's documentation and the response assessment is that organisation's; the 2024-25 adolescent rulings are as reported and not independently re-verified here. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

Blind drops country name, city names, organisation names, 'South/Latin America' and bare 'state' wording.

rewrites.summary:
Cambodia is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — the country has never criminalised same-sex activity or gender expression — and the government is formally cooperative: it accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations at its 2024 Universal Periodic Review, including legal gender recognition, and hosted the UN Independent Expert on SOGI in 2023. Phnom Penh and Siem Reap, the country's two main cities, have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors.

The risks are street-level and police-level rather than legal: a human-rights organisation documents "shocking" harassment and abuse of transgender women in urban centres, including a reported police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse). There is no legal gender recognition yet, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute.

For a visitor: low probability of legal trouble; moderate probability of harassment if visibly trans outside tourist areas; police are a risk factor, not a protection, for trans women especially.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The cooperative posture carries an unfulfilled-promise edge: the country also accepted recommendations to legalise same-sex marriage (2019 review) and seven on marriage equality (2024 review), and legislation still contains no SOGI non-discrimination provisions — a reform-promise layer rather than a visitor-facing restriction.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The LGR absence and discrimination-law gaps are resident-facing; the Siem Reap police extortion practice primarily affects resident trans women.

The documented harassment and abuse cases describe resident trans women on city streets, and the police practice of targeting resident trans sex workers is the sharpest resident-facing manifestation.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence and discrimination-law gaps are resident-facing. The police-practice reports are reported but not adjudicated by any court in this record; the expert-visit findings are summarised from the hosting organisation's page and not independently re-verified here. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

rewrites.summary:
Mongolia is a country workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 1993, discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, and identity grounds were added to the hate-crime provisions of the Criminal Code in 2015. There are no bathroom laws, no border/document friction for foreign passports, and no police targeting pattern; police guidance requires officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of identification documents, a favourable enforcement practice.

The realistic risk for a visitor is street harassment if visibly trans, particularly at night and outside the capital's central districts, where social acceptance is low.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Institutional work is the adjacent layer: an organised community successfully lobbied for the hate-crime protections, and after an officer assaulted a detained transgender woman, the police force was trained on the hate-crime provisions of the 2017 code — hundreds of officers, prosecutors and judges — a documented training response to an enforcement failure.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The medicalised LGR process and the fragmented anti-discrimination protections are resident-facing; the LGBT Centre assault documentation describes residents' experience.

An older account (2008) described the resident scene as having virtually no presence, venues or activism, with two organisations holding furtive monthly gatherings where attendees feared being outed.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Comprehensive anti-discrimination gaps and medicalised LGR are resident-facing. The assault documentation and the training figures are from reporting sources and have not been independently re-verified in this record; the older scene account describes 2008 conditions. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

blindSourceSummaries: A profile of this country (updated March 2026) records that consensual same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 1993, that identity-based discrimination is prohibited but protections are fragmented (no comprehensive law), that marriage equality is constitutionally barred with no union recognition, and that groups can register.
thin: no usable finding

A profile piece (August 2018) describes a trans man who advises the community centre, and describes a pride gathering and the centre's advocacy; it is ground on trans life, transition access and acceptance in the capital.

A news report (October 2019) records that after an officer assaulted a detained transgender woman, the police were trained on the 2017 criminal code's hate-crime provisions — hundreds of officers, prosecutors and judges trained; guidelines now require officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of identification documents.

A travel-community report records that no laws specifically target homosexuality, though provisions on immoral sexual needs remain; the scene has virtually no presence, venues or activism, with a 2008 account describing two organisations holding furtive monthly parties where attendees feared being outed.

rewrites.summary:
Nepal is workable for trans visitors — South Asia's most legally recognising country. The Supreme Court has protected gender identity since a landmark 2007 ruling; a third-gender category exists on documents by self-identification; and in 2024 the Supreme Court ruled that a trans woman must be recognised as female without medical verification. Nothing is criminalised, and Kathmandu, the capital, has an established activist scene.

The gap between doctrine and practice is large: an international observer, Human Rights Watch, documents that implementation is piecemeal and humiliating, and trans people in provinces face physical and sexual harassment in public spaces with little police protection. These burdens fall overwhelmingly on residents navigating citizenship documents — a visitor with a foreign passport faces none of the bureaucratic gauntlet.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, tolerant tourist areas, but expect stares and possible harassment if visibly trans outside the main tourist bubbles.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Doctrine-versus-implementation commentary is the adjacent factor: a news analysis in The Diplomat (2024) argues the country's progressive reputation outruns its policy, since officials limited changes to people identifying as third-gender while male/female marker changes lagged. The 2007 ruling was novel at the time and later cases reinforced it, but no straightforward document-change process exists despite the progressive rulings.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The third-gender "O" category, the Rukshana Kapali ruling, and the HRW-documented implementation failures all concern residents navigating citizenship documents.

The landmark 2007 ruling, the third-gender category by self-identification, and the harassment documented in provincial cities all fall on residents; the established activist scene (an organisation founded 2001) is resident-facing.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Documentation barriers are resident-facing; citizenship-law discrimination does not affect visitors. The citizenship-document process after the rulings is not independently verified in this record; the documented failures date from the 2024 observer report and the 2024 ruling account. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

blindSourceSummaries: An international observer's report (February 2024) calls on the government to create a clear, simple, rights-respecting procedure so transgender and third-gender people can obtain official documents, illustrating that despite progressive rulings no straightforward document-change process exists.

A news report (August 2024) records that the supreme court ruled a trans woman must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed many lawsuits; previously, changing markers usually required surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations.

A news analysis (February 2024) argues that the 2007 ruling allowing self-identified legal gender was novel at the time and later cases reinforced it, but officials limited changes to people identifying as third-gender while male/female marker changes lagged — the country's progressive reputation outruns its policy.

A news feature (November 2024) records ground-level conditions for visibly trans people in provincial cities: discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions, and frequent physical and sexual harassment.
A community publication (October 2021) records a civil-society draft bill on legal gender recognition.

A contributor analysis (September 2020) argues that despite the constitutional right to self-determine name and gender markers, an extensive overhaul of the law is still needed to address inequalities.
A study-abroad paper (2015) records that despite changing legislation, sexual and gender minorities face deeply rooted stigma and obstacles in nearly every arena of life.
rewrites.notes: Preserved current localsOnly and outOfScopeNotes and extended them; observer/reputation commentary to tangential; ruling names and founding story kept visible and dropped in blind; 'South Asia' and city names removed from blind; identity-first legal posture kept.
